_comment: The repository settings a repository on these standards is expected to have.
Applied by .github/scripts/apply-settings.py, which reads before it writes and
previews by default. Every value here is required by something documented:
the reason is in the _why block beside its group, and a setting nothing
needs is not here.
SETTINGS ONLY. Branch and tag protection live in data/rulesets/ and are
applied separately, because they are the change that can lock you out.
Four groups, one plan. `repository` is the repository object, one PATCH.
`actions` is Settings → Actions: everything under General, each key its
own endpoint, and one event policy under Policies, found by its name.
`security` is the Advanced Security page, each feature its own endpoint
or its own status on the repository object. `releases` is the Releases
section of Settings → General.
Everything writable that is deliberately NOT here is in _excluded, with
the reason - absence is always a decision, never an oversight. Most of it
can still be written from a settings-file override; _excluded says how.
Some settings are gated on visibility or plan, and the script skips those
with a notice rather than failing: a repository that cannot have a feature
has not misconfigured anything. A setting the repository does not report
at all is skipped the same way, never guessed at.

_why.allow_squash_merge: Squash is the only door. The rulesets set allowed_merge_methods to squash on every protected branch; this makes the button agree.
_why.allow_merge_commit: A merge commit has no Conventional Commit subject, so the changelog generator cannot see it.
_why.allow_rebase_merge: Rebase replays commits individually, which puts unsquashed work-in-progress subjects on a protected branch.
_why.squash_merge_commit_title: The pull request title becomes the commit that lands, which is exactly what semantic-pr.yml validates.
_why.squash_merge_commit_message: The pull request body becomes the commit body, which is how the required commit body arrives without retyping it.
_why.delete_branch_on_merge: Documented in Repository-Hygiene as the on-merge cadence. Nothing else prunes merged heads.
_why.allow_auto_merge: REQUIRED, not cosmetic. dependabot-automerge.yml and open-pr.sh both call `gh pr merge --auto`, which fails without it.
_why.allow_update_branch: Lets a pull request take the base branch without a merge commit, so strict required checks can be satisfied.
_why.web_commit_signoff_required: The DCO check requires a Signed-off-by trailer on every human commit; this makes edits made in the browser comply instead of failing.
_why.has_issues: The issue forms, the label taxonomy, and the intake chooser are all fronted by Issues. It is on by default everywhere; this puts it back if it was ever turned off.
_why.has_discussions: SUPPORT.md and the issue chooser route questions to Discussions, and the chooser's link 404s until this is on. The public template ships the discussion forms it expects.
_why.has_wiki: Documentation is versioned in the tree and reviewed. A wiki is neither.
_why.has_projects: Off by default rather than opinionated: turn it on deliberately if you use it.

_why_actions.permissions.enabled: Actions is how every standard here reaches a repository: the checks, the governance, the release chain. A repository with it off has none of them, and this run cannot even be dispatched there; it exists so a hand-run from a clone puts it back.
_why_actions.permissions.sha_pinning_required: FALSE ON PURPOSE. GitHub's SHA-pinning requirement covers every action reference, and the stubs reach the composite actions published here as tannergolden/standards/actions/<name>@v1 - a tag, by design, so a fix reaches every repository at once. With the requirement on, every one of those references is refused and every workflow fails. The actions those composites wrap are pinned by SHA already; the moving tag is the one layer that cannot be.
_why_actions.permissions.allowed_actions: NOT WRITTEN, deliberately. An allowlist is real hardening with a real maintenance bill, and a repository that chose one by hand must not have it undone by a sync. Set it from an override: `allowed_actions: "selected"` with a `selected_actions` block, and the script applies both.
_why_actions.workflow.default_workflow_permissions: READ, GitHub's own default for a new repository in a personal account. It is the token a job gets when it declares no permissions, and it caps nothing that declares them: anyone with write access sets the token for a job with the permissions key in its workflow file, adding or removing access as the job needs. Every workflow published here, and every stub in tannergolden/path, declares that key for every job, so each runs with exactly what it declares. Read-only protects the workflow that forgets: one with no permissions key can read and do nothing more. It satisfies OpenSSF Baseline OSPS-AC-04.01, and clears the OpenSSF SCM best-practice check token_default_permissions_is_read_write.
_why_actions.workflow.can_approve_pull_request_review: TRUE while required approvals stay at the shipped 0. It lets the built-in token open pull requests and approve them: open-pr.sh opens the pull requests of auto-format, auto-index and template sync as github-actions, and dependabot-automerge.yml approves Dependabot's. Without it each needs a BOT_ACCESS_TOKEN, or can only tell you to come flip it by hand. At 0 required approvals an approval from a workflow decides nothing; at 1 or more it is a way around review, since a workflow can approve a pull request in a reviewer's place. So raise required approvals together with an override that turns this off, and supply a BOT_ACCESS_TOKEN for the automation to use instead.
_why_actions.fork_pr_contributor_approval: ALL EXTERNAL CONTRIBUTORS: a fork pull request from anyone outside the repository waits for a maintainer to approve its workflow runs, however many of their pull requests have merged before. GitHub's secure-use reference and the CIS Software Supply Chain Security Guide (2.3.5) recommend it for public repositories, because a first-time policy is satisfied by one merged typo fix, and every pull request from that account after it runs its workflows unreviewed. The cost is a click per run: the required checks on such a pull request start once a maintainer approves them. PUBLIC repositories only: GitHub refuses the endpoint on a private repository, which an outsider cannot fork, so the run skips it with a notice there.
_why_actions.fork_pr_workflows_private_repos: PRIVATE repositories only, skipped with a notice elsewhere. A private repository's collaborators push topic branches to the repository itself, which is what the branching strategy describes, so a workflow from a fork of it has no business running at all - and certainly not with a write token or the secrets. Approval is required for the case where one does.
_why_actions.access_level: PRIVATE repositories only, skipped with a notice elsewhere. This is whether workflows in OTHER repositories may call the actions and reusable workflows inside this one. These standards publish shared workflows from one public repository, so nothing needs to reach into a private one, and `none` closes a door nothing uses.
_why_actions.event_policy: PUBLIC repositories only, skipped with a notice elsewhere. GitHub has added a default policy that blocks the pull_request_target event in every public repository without an applicable Actions event policy, enforced from 2 December 2026, and a run it blocks fails with an error. The governance stub's pull request triage and first-time welcome write labels and comments on a fork's pull request, which takes pull_request_target, so this policy allows the event for that one file and no other. That is safe because the file never checks out pull-request code: its jobs read and write through the API, and the one checkout behind it takes the base branch. An event rule is an allowlist, so the list names every event the file uses, and a trigger added to the stub but missing here is blocked for it. workflow_call is allowed too, though the stub declares no such trigger and nothing can call it: the shared workflow it calls for triage sits at the same path in the standards, and GitHub does not say which file it checks a called workflow's rule against, so allowing the event keeps that call running either way. A stub kept under another name needs its own path, from an override.
_why_actions.artifact_and_log_retention_days: GitHub's default and the most a public repository allows, written so a shortened window shows up as drift. Since October 2026 this window also deletes checks, workflow runs and commit statuses, so shortening it costs a long-lived pull request its checks. Trimming runs below the window is prune-runs.yml's job, which keeps recent history and anything in flight; retention is a blunt instrument by comparison.

_why_security.secret_scanning: Security-&-Secrets names it as the platform-native layer beside Gitleaks. Free on a public repository; on a private one it needs GitHub Secret Protection, and the run skips it with a notice until the repository reports the feature.
_why_security.secret_scanning_push_protection: Stops a credential at the boundary rather than reporting it afterwards. Gated like secret scanning: free on public, Secret Protection on private.
_why_security.secret_scanning_non_provider_patterns: Widens platform scanning past provider tokens to generic credentials - private keys, connection strings - the same class Gitleaks hunts from the other side. Plan-gated even on public repositories: written only where the repository reports the feature, skipped with a notice everywhere else.
_why_security.secret_scanning_ai_detection: Copilot secret scanning: the detector for unstructured secrets such as passwords, beside the non-provider patterns for structured ones. Plan-gated the same way, and written only where the repository reports the feature; a refusal is a notice, not a failure.
_why_security.vulnerability_alerts: Dependabot alerts, which also turn on the dependency graph. The dependency-management standard assumes they are on. Compared before it is written, like everything else: GitHub answers 204 when it is on and 404 when it is not.
_why_security.automated_security_fixes: Dependabot security updates, which is what opens the pull requests that dependabot-automerge.yml then handles. Needs the alerts above, which are applied first.
_why_security.private_vulnerability_reporting: Gives the Security tab a Report a vulnerability entry, which is the intake SECURITY.md points at. A public-repository feature; skipped with a notice on a private one.
_why_security.code_scanning_default_setup: NOT-CONFIGURED ON PURPOSE. The code scanning these standards ship is the codeql.yml stub, an advanced setup that detects the repository's languages itself. GitHub's default setup overrides an advanced one: it disables the existing CodeQL workflow and rejects its uploads, so a repository with both has a stub that silently stops reporting. Turning default setup off here keeps the stub the one scanner. Skipped with a notice where code scanning is unavailable, which is a private repository without GitHub Code Security.

_why_releases.immutable: FALSE ON PURPOSE, and only while the shipped release chain works the way it does. An immutable release refuses any change to its assets and tag after publication, and release-publish.yml builds and attaches the artifacts AFTER a drafted release is published, on the `release: published` trigger. With immutability on, that upload is refused and every release ships without its tarball or SBOM. A repository that publishes its assets before it publishes the release can turn this on from an override; the run then reports it as drift nowhere, because an override is the standard for that repository.

_excluded._comment: Every writable repository setting that is deliberately NOT here, so absence is always a decision and never an oversight. Where an override can write one, the key to use is named. The complete map, including what generation sets and what has no API at all, is docs/operations/Repository-Settings.md.
_excluded.name, description, homepage, topics: Identity. Initialisation rewrites what the template stamped; what the project is called and about is yours, and a shared value would overwrite it on every run. (An override may still carry `name`, `description` or `homepage` under `repository`.)
_excluded.private / visibility: Changing who can see a repository is a human act with legal and billing consequences, never a side effect of a settings sync. The script refuses these keys in any file.
_excluded.archived, is_template, default_branch: Structural state. Generation inherits the default branch (Development) from the template; archiving and templating are one-time decisions. The script refuses `archived` and `default_branch` in any file.
_excluded.has_pull_requests, pull_request_creation: Two new fields on the repository object - whether pull requests are on at all, and whether only collaborators may open them. What the API reports for them does not yet match what a repository does: a repository that merges pull requests weekly reads `has_pull_requests: false`. Left alone until it does. Writable from an override under `repository` once you have checked what your repositories report.
_excluded.allow_forking: Exists only on organization-owned private repositories; personal public repositories are always forkable. Writable from an override under `repository`.
_excluded.advanced_security / code_security: Paid per committer on private repositories. Billing decisions belong to a person, so the script only uses security features where they are already available. An override may set `code_security: true` or `advanced_security: true` under `security` on a repository that pays for them.
_excluded.secret_scanning_delegated_bypass, secret: Organization-owned repositories with Secret Protection, and the bypass reviewers are named people, which no shared file can know. An override may set either under `security`; the reviewer list stays a manual act.
_excluded.merge_commit_title, merge_commit_message: They configure a door this standard nails shut: allow_merge_commit is false, so no one could ever see these values.
_excluded.actions.permissions.allowed_actions, act: An action allowlist is deliberate hardening a sync must not undo. See _why_actions for how an override turns one on.
_excluded.actions.cache_retention_days, actions.ca: Actions cache retention and size limits. Plan-gated (a payment method or a paid plan) and GitHub's defaults of 7 days and 10 GB fit everything here. Both writable from an override under `actions`; the run skips them with a notice where the plan lacks them.
_excluded.environments: Protection rules name human reviewers, which no shared file can know, and the first deploy creates the environment it names. The manual-hardening list in docs/operations/Repository-Settings.md covers setting them up.
_excluded.pages, webhooks, autolinks, deploy keys,: Project-specific wiring with no standard value.
_excluded.interaction_limits, pull request creatio: Temporary moderation levers by design; a sync that re-applied them would turn an incident response into permanent policy.
_excluded.other Actions policies, code quality set: Organization, enterprise or plan features with no standard value for a repository on these standards. The one Actions policy that has one, the event policy for the governance stub, is under `actions`; any other, such as an actor rule, names people or workflows no shared file can know.
